In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the swine herds in South Korea are under constant pressure from swine influenza viruses of three distinct subtypes, H1N1, H1N2 and H3N2, which have undergone independent and multiple reassortments in recent years.
the H1N1 subtype has been eradicated from the Korean swine population while the H1N3 and H1N2 subtypes are still co-circulating.
the H1N1 and H3N2 subtypes have co-circulated in Korea since 2000 and the H1N3 and H3N1 subtypes have been isolated from pigs in Korea since 1998.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
swine herds in South Korea have been exposed to all three influenza subtypes and that the H1N1 subtype has disappeared from the swine population.

swine herds in South Korea have been experiencing a natural infection of H1 and H2 subtypes since 1999 and the vaccination program has been successful in reducing the incidence of H1N1 and H3N2 subtypes.
the swine influenza virus in Korean swine population is currently co-circulated by H1N1, H1N2, and H3N2 subtypes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the swine influenza viruses are evolving in Korean swines by multiple reassortment events, and that the H1N1 and H3N2 viruses have become genetically diverse and are circulating in Korean swine population.
the swine influenza vaccine used in South Korea has not been effective in preventing the emergence of novel reassortant strains.

the current vaccination strategy in Korean swine industry has not been effective in controlling swine influenza virus circulation and that the vaccination should be reevaluated to prevent the emergence and spread of novel swine influenza viruses.
